slides.title: A planted roof takes on three new jobs
slides.title_html:
A planted roof takes on
three new jobs
slides.subtitle: Most city roofs only keep the rain out. Planting keeps that job and adds three more.

backdrop.alt: Tall grasses and wildflowers on a roof between historic office buildings

slides.body_html:
01 · Cool

Shade the roof

Plants shade the surface and release water vapour, so the rooms below stay cooler in summer.

02 · Hold

Slow the rain

The growing layer soaks up a storm and lets it go slowly, easing the load on drains.

03 · Host

Make room for life

Bees, butterflies and birds find food and shelter between the towers.
slides.notes_en: Three jobs, one sentence each. Keep it qualitative; add local figures only from a source you can cite.

slides.title: Three kinds of green roof
slides.body_html:
01

Extensive

A thin carpet of sedum and moss. Light, and needs little care.

02

Intensive

Deeper soil for shrubs and trees: a garden people can use.

03

Rooftop farm

Beds and rows for food, run by a business or a community.
slides.notes_en: Depth decides everything: weight, cost, what grows and who can use it.

slides.title: Four questions before you plant
slides.subtitle: Answer these with the building's owner and an engineer.

backdrop.alt: Grasses and flowers on a city roof

slides.body_html:
1Can the roof carry it?

Wet soil is heavy. Ask a structural engineer first.

2How will people get up?

Access for care, materials and, for gardens, visitors.

3Where does the water go?

Drains, overflow, and whether plants need watering.

4Who looks after it?

A named owner and a care plan, from the start.
